records.title: AP3: the traversal makes one query per node — loading all 108 731 edges costs less than 1 000 incident lookups
records.body:
AP3 from the mandate. **Two variants with measured numbers, as instructed — the choice is yours, not
mine.**

> Entscheidungsregel: Lege beide Varianten mit gemessenen Zahlen aus F3 vor und lass die Wahl
> bestätigen. Nicht selbst entscheiden.

## F3 — the trigger fires, and it is worse than "one query per level"

`BlastRadiusTool` calls `GetIncidentEdgesAsync(cur)` **once per visited node** inside its BFS
(`BlastRadiusTool.cs:101`), not once per level. `ReferencesTool`'s transitive branch does the same
(`AnalyzeTools.cs:91`).

Measured on live `sitecoreMuM` (108 731 edges, 26 958 nodes):

| operation | time |
|---|---|
| `GetAllEdgesAsync` — the whole edge set | **1 018 ms**, ~70 MB retained |
| `GetIncidentEdgesAsync` × 1 000 | **1 299 ms** (1,30 ms per call), 45 083 edges seen |

**Loading every edge in the graph costs less than a thousand incident lookups**, and those thousand see
less than half the edges — with duplicates.

A depth-5 traversal reaching 7 046 nodes (the pre-AP7 figure for one real class) spends
7 046 × 1,30 ms ≈ **9,2 seconds in roundtrips alone**. After AP7's default exclusion the same traversal
reaches 92 nodes, so the cost is currently hidden by a filter rather than absent — and `includeModelEdges=true`
brings all of it back.

## Variant A — one `WITH RECURSIVE` statement

Reverse reachability plus weakest-tier aggregation in a single SQL statement.

- One roundtrip regardless of depth or breadth.
- Memory stays SQLite's problem.
- The tier/reason/model filters move into SQL. All three are already expressed as sets, so this is
  mechanical — but it puts the AP2 and AP7 semantics into a second language, and *"two ways to express
  one constraint"* is the shape that produced #399's 1 354 stranded edges.
- Recursive CTE termination on a cyclic graph needs care; the current BFS terminates via
  relax-on-improvement, which does not translate directly.

## Variant B — in-process adjacency, SQLite as persistence only

Load the edge set once, traverse in memory.

- **70 MB for the largest graph here**, loaded in 1 second. `FPM-Optimizely` is roughly half that.
- Filters stay in C#, where AP2/AP7 already live. One implementation, one set of tests.
- Cost is per *process*, not per query: the MCP stdio server pays it once at startup and every later
  traversal is free. The HTTP relay is per-request and would pay it every time — that is the case that
  decides against a naive version.
- Staleness: an in-memory copy goes stale the moment a scan writes. #449's revision marker gives a cheap
  invalidation signal, but it has to be wired.

## What I would want you to weigh

The honest asymmetry: **A** is one roundtrip but a second implementation of the filter semantics;
**B** is one implementation but a cache with a lifetime question. This project's recurring defect has
been two components disagreeing about the same thing — which argues for B — while its other recurring
defect has been state that outlives its validity, which argues for A.

I have no measurement that settles that, and the mandate says not to decide it myself.

Nothing built.

records.title: Replace group hierarchy BFS N+1 queries with recursive CTEs
records.body:
## Summary

The group hierarchy traversals in `pkg/store/entadapter/group_store.go` use application-level BFS with one query per tree level (N+1 pattern). These can be replaced with single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE queries, eliminating per-level round trips.

## Current state

Two BFS functions in `group_store.go:745-828`:

### `hasPathDown()` (~line 745)
Walks `child_groups` edge downward to check if a path exists between two groups. Max depth 10. Each BFS step issues:
```go
s.client.Group.Query().Where(...).QueryChildGroups().All(ctx)
```
One query per level of the tree.

### `GetEffectiveGroups()` (~line 800)
BFS upward through `parent_groups` to collect all ancestor groups for a user's memberships. Same N+1 pattern — one query per level.

Both are bounded at 10 levels, so the worst case is 10 sequential queries per call. In practice, group hierarchies are typically 2-4 levels deep.

## Proposed fix

Replace each BFS with a single `WITH RECURSIVE` CTE:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE ancestors AS (
    SELECT parent_group_id FROM group_children WHERE child_group_id = $1
    UNION
    SELECT gc.parent_group_id FROM group_children gc
    JOIN ancestors a ON gc.child_group_id = a.parent_group_id
)
SELECT id FROM groups WHERE id IN (SELECT parent_group_id FROM ancestors);
```

This is standard SQL supported by both PostgreSQL and SQLite (SQLite has supported `WITH RECURSIVE` since 3.8.3 / 2014), so dual-dialect compatibility is maintained.

## Why this instead of PG19 SQL/PGQ

A strategic assessment of PG19's new SQL/PGQ graph query support concluded that Scion's graph traversals are too shallow (mostly 1-2 hops) and PG19's graph indexing too immature to justify adoption. Recursive CTEs solve the only concrete N+1 performance issue today, with no version dependency.

Assessment: `scratchpad/projects/roadmap/inv-pg19-graph-ent-assessment.md`

## Files

- `pkg/store/entadapter/group_store.go:745-828` — the BFS functions to replace
- `pkg/hub/authz_delegation_ceiling.go` — delegation chain walk (similar pattern but operates on flat table, lower priority)
- `pkg/store/entadapter/dialect.go` — existing dialect-specific SQL patterns (reference for CTE integration)

records.title: [A-08.02] Learn graph reps + the 4 templates — 0:40
records.body:
Sub-block of chunk **[A-08] Graphs: Grids, Union-Find & Topological Sort** ([`A-08-graphs.md`](https://github.com/kenziedrysdale/dsa-problems/blob/master/A-08-graphs.md)).

**Three representations** — know all three cold:
- **Adjacency list** (default for sparse graphs).
- **Adjacency matrix** (dense graphs / O(1) edge lookup).
- **Implicit grid graph** — neighbors are up/down/left/right (and sometimes diagonals); no explicit edge list.

**Four templates to reproduce from a blank screen:**
1. **BFS** (queue + visited set) — shortest path in an *unweighted* graph, level expansion, multi-source fill.
2. **DFS** (recursive *and* iterative) — connectivity, cycle detection, flood fill.
3. **Union-Find** with **path compression + union by rank** — dynamic connectivity, counting components; near-O(α(n)) per op.
4. **Topological sort** — both **Kahn's (BFS over in-degrees)** and **DFS post-order**; a cycle ⇒ no valid topo order (so topo sort doubles as cycle detection on a DAG).

For every grid problem define four things up front: **what's a node, what's an edge, what counts as "visited," and the boundary conditions.** Skipping this is where grid bugs come from.

> **Learn it from the source:** CP-Algorithms (cp-algorithms.com) **Graph** section — the BFS, DFS, connected-components, *DSU (Disjoint Set Union)*, and *topological sort* articles are the cleanest reference implementations anywhere. Sedgewick & Wayne, *Algorithms* (4th ed.) **Part II / Ch. 4 "Graphs"** (Undirected/Directed Graphs, plus its free booksite algs4.cs.princeton.edu and the **Princeton Algorithms Coursera Part II**). Skiena, *The Algorithm Design Manual* (3rd ed.) Ch. 5–7 (graph traversal, weighted graphs) for the *modeling* instinct — "what is the graph here?"

records.title: Implement extends schema relationship with real node_type subtype identity
records.body:
## Overview

NodeSpace has no way for one schema to declare "I am a task, plus these additional fields," and no way for an instance of such a schema to report its real, specific type via node_type. This issue implements ../nodespace-docs/decisions/078-schema-extends-relationship-for-field-composition.md (ADR-078) in full: a new extends SchemaRelationship, real node_type-as-extending-type for created instances, and the query-engine/trigger-engine/write-path changes required to make that safe.

## Problem Statement

A schema extending task today can only restate every field task already has — there is no composition mechanism, and no way for a node created under such a schema to report anything other than node_type: "task". This blocks any methodology-recipe or domain-specific specialization (a Linear-style "Issue" extending task, a marketing "campaign_task" extending task) from having real, queryable, trigger-matchable type identity distinct from its base type.

## Architecture Impact

This issue implements `../nodespace-docs/decisions/078-schema-extends-relationship-for-field-composition.md` (ADR-078) in full — Status: Proposed, becomes Accepted once implemented and merged per this repo's ADR convention. ADR-078 itself reversed an earlier, narrower version of its own design (kept `node_type` as the base type) after four rounds of architect review found that version couldn't satisfy the real requirement (a node's own `node_type` should tell the truth about what it is). Read ADR-078's Context/Revision-history section for the full reasoning and the two intermediate designs it rejects.

This issue also relies on `../nodespace-docs/decisions/075-playbooknode-installable-bundle-record.md` (ADR-075) having already dropped its `kinds[]` mechanism — ADR-075 has been rewritten to no longer describe `kinds[]`/`derived_from_playbook`/`_extension_kind` at all (they were never implemented, so removed outright rather than deprecated, per this repo's pre-release convention). No code implements any of that mechanism today, so there is nothing to delete in this repo — this note exists so an implementer doesn't go looking for it.

## Proposed Solution

Add `extends` as a structurally-reserved `SchemaRelationship`. A schema declaring `extends` composes its effective field set as its own fields plus its parent's (additive only, single parent, no override). An instance created under an extending schema gets that schema's own id as its real `node_type`. The query engine and trigger engine are made subtype-aware via cheap recursive-CTE closures over the `relationship` table (the same `WITH RECURSIVE` pattern already proven in production for `MENTION_CONTAINERS_QUERY` and the collection-subtree query), implemented at single choke points so no existing call site needs individual changes.

## Acceptance Criteria

### Schema layer
- [ ] `extends` and `extended_by` added to `BUILTIN_RELATIONSHIP_NAMES` (`packages/core/src/models/schema.rs`)
- [ ] `create_schema`/`update_schema` accept an `extends` `SchemaRelationship` declaration (direction `out`, cardinality `one`, reverse `extended_by`/`many`), persisted via the existing `set_schema_declarations` path
- [ ] Target-existence validation reuses `validate_relationship_targets_exist`
- [ ] Cycle detection: a DFS/visited-set walk over the `extends` chain, run at both `create_schema` and `update_schema` time, rejecting `A extends B extends A` (test: direct cycle, transitive cycle through 2+ intermediate schemas)
- [ ] Cardinality enforcement: a second `extends` declaration on the same schema is rejected (test)
- [ ] No-field-redeclaration validation checked against the full resolved effective field set (own ∪ every ancestor's), not just the schema's own directly-declared fields (test: redeclaring an inherited field, including an inherited enum field with different `core_values`, is rejected)
- [ ] `resolve_effective_fields(schema_id) -> Vec<SchemaField>` resolver implemented, reading parent schemas live (or through a cache correctly invalidated on any write to a schema anywhere in the chain) — test that a value appended to a parent's enum field via `add_field_values` is visible in a child's resolved fields on next resolution, without touching the child
- [ ] `get_schema_definition`/schema-comprehension consumers use the resolver instead of a schema's own directly-declared `fields`

### Real node_type
- [ ] Creating an instance of a schema declaring `extends` produces a node with `node_type` equal to that schema's own id (not the base type) — test
- [ ] `create_node`/`update_node`'s schema-fetch feeding `validate_node_with_fields` (currently a single, non-chain-walking `get_schema_for_type` call) switches to the effective-field-set resolver, so creating an `issue`-typed node correctly validates/defaults `task`'s inherited fields — test

### Query engine
- [ ] A descendant-closure `WITH RECURSIVE` query (walking `out_node → in_node` on `relationship_type = 'extends'` edges, modeled directly on `MENTION_CONTAINERS_QUERY`/the collection-subtree query in `packages/core/src/db/sqlite_store/relationships.rs`) resolves a base type's full transitive subtype set
- [ ] This closure is resolved once, inside `build_scalar_conditions` (`packages/core/src/db/sqlite_store/nodes.rs`), compiling `node_type = ?` into `node_type IN (...)` — test: querying `node_type: "task"` returns instances of `task` and every schema transitively extending it, with zero changes to any of the callers that construct `NodeQuery`
- [ ] Querying the leaf type directly (`node_type: "issue"`) continues to return exactly `issue` instances (test — confirms the expansion is additive, not lossy)

### Trigger engine
- [ ] An ancestor-closure `WITH RECURSIVE` query (walking `in_node → out_node`) resolves a specific node_type's full ancestry
- [ ] This closure is cached in `PlaybookLifecycleManager` (`packages/core/src/playbook/lifecycle.rs`), not queried per mutation event — test or diagnostic confirming trigger match

records.title: Crafting using environmental sources (water, honey, ecto mist, etc.) doesn't work with recursive crafting enabled
records.body:
When recursion depth is set to anything but 0, attempting to craft an item that is made from an environmental source does nothing – the crafting sound is made, but no materials are consumed, nor is the item actually created.

I've encountered this attempting to craft Flymeal, Gravedigger's Shovel, Bottled Water, and any potion that has a crafting tree that goes through Bottled Water (i.e. not healing potions), so the environmental source seems to be the common factor.

records.title: coordinator: a query that reads a recursive CTE fails on the DAG with the stage builder's own message ('stage scan-0 has no dependencies and no ScanFiles') instead of a local route or 0A000
records.body:
Measured by the A2 round-8 Opus author on all three DAG arms (dag, dag-shuffled, dag-morsel4) with a VALID query and no TCP-flag function in it, at 404b65a0 and pinned on its branch as `coordinator.…/control/recursive_cte_*`; the round-7 reviewer's arm log carries the identical message. Pre-existing.

**Shape:** `WITH RECURSIVE r(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM r WHERE n < 5) SELECT n FROM r` — single-process answers five rows; the distributed path fails with

```
stage scan-0 has no dependencies and no ScanFiles
```

That is the stage builder describing a plan it cannot express, surfaced as an internal error with no SQLSTATE. The single-process engine materializes recursive CTEs (`physical.materializeRecursiveCTE`); the DAG has no equivalent and does not route the query local the way it routes scalar-subquery projections and table-less selects (`ScalarProjectionLocalRoutes`, `ErrTableLessSelectDistributed`).

**Expected:** either the coordinator routes a query holding a recursive CTE to the in-process pipeline (the fast-path contract of #308: a local failure that says nothing about the query's meaning falls back; a plan shape the DAG cannot stage is exactly that), or it refuses with 0A000 naming the feature. A stage-builder message is neither.

**Gate:** the pin the author added flips when the DAG learns to run one; add the routed-flag assertion (`UnreachableOutputLocalRoutes`/a new counter) when the local route lands. Related: #1041 (the materializer discards execution errors).

records.title: Code Review: Session 3 - Stories & Comments API
records.body:
## Overview
Review REST API design, query optimization, and testing patterns. This establishes API conventions for the project.

**Depends on**: #3 must be completed, #17 (Session 2 review) completed  
**Session**: Week 1, Session 3  
**Focus**: API design, query performance, error handling, testing patterns

---

## Code Quality Checklist

### API Design
- [ ] **REST conventions**: Proper HTTP methods and status codes?
- [ ] **Pagination**: Using limit/offset or cursor-based? Default limits set?
- [ ] **Response models**: Using Pydantic models for response validation?
- [ ] **Request validation**: Query params validated (limit max value, offset >= 0)?
- [ ] **Consistent structure**: All responses follow same envelope pattern?
- [ ] **Error responses**: Consistent error format (RFC 7807 or custom)?

### Database Queries
- [ ] **Connection pooling**: Using connection pool not new connection per request?
- [ ] **SQL injection**: Using parameterized queries everywhere?
- [ ] **N+1 queries**: Are comments fetched in single query not loop?
- [ ] **Proper indexing**: Queries use indexes (check with EXPLAIN)?
- [ ] **Query timeout**: Configured to prevent runaway queries?

### Error Handling
- [ ] **404 handling**: Story not found returns 404 not 500?
- [ ] **500 errors**: Database errors caught and logged appropriately?
- [ ] **Validation errors**: Return 422 with clear error messages?
- [ ] **Exception handlers**: Global exception handlers configured?

### Code Organization
- [ ] **Routers**: Using APIRouter for organization not monolithic main.py?
- [ ] **Dependency injection**: Database connections via Depends()?
- [ ] **Separation of concerns**: Business logic separated from route handlers?

---

## Design Review Questions

### API Design Choices
1. **Pagination strategy**: Why limit/offset vs cursor-based? What are the tradeoffs?
   ```
   Limit/offset: Simple but slow for deep pagination
   Cursor: Fast but complex, no random page access
   ```
2. **Default limits**: What default limit was chosen? Why? HN uses 30 items per page.
3. **Sorting**: Stories sorted by `score DESC, time DESC`. Why this order? Should it be configurable?
4. **Response structure**: Show the actual JSON response shape. Is it:
   ```json
   // Option A: Direct array
   [{"id": 1, ...}, {"id": 2, ...}]
   
   // Option B: Envelope
   {"data": [...], "total": 1234, "offset": 0, "limit": 20}
   ```
   Which is better? Why?

5. **Comment nesting**: Are comments returned flat or nested tree structure?
   ```json
   // Flat (easier to implement)
   [{"id": 1, "parent_id": null}, {"id": 2, "parent_id": 1}]
   
   // Nested (better for frontend)
   [{"id": 1, "replies": [{"id": 2, "replies": []}]}]
   ```
   Which was chosen? Show the code that builds this.

### Query Optimization
6. **Indexes used**: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on queries. Are indexes being used?
7. **Query efficiency**: For `/stories/{id}/comments`, how are comments retrieved?
   - Single recursive CTE query?
   - Multiple queries?
   - Plain SELECT with post-processing?
8. **Performance targets**: What's acceptable latency for these endpoints?
   - `/stories`: < 100ms?
   - `/stories/{id}`: < 50ms?
   - `/stories/{id}/comments`: < 200ms?

### Database Connection Management
9. **Connection lifecycle**: How are connections acquired and released? Show the code.
10. **Pool configuration**: What's the connection pool size? Why?
11. **Session management**: Are sessions properly closed on errors?

---

## Integration & Compatibility

### Session 1-2 Integration
- [ ] **Config consistency**: Uses same environment variables as Sessions 1-2?
- [ ] **Database schema**: Works with schema from Session 2 without changes?
- [ ] **Docker workflow**: API runs in container, can connect to PostgreSQL?

### Future Sessions
- [ ] **Session 4 summaries**: Can the `GET /stories/{id}` response accommodate a summary field?
- [ ] **Session 5 search**: Is the response structure compatible with search results?
- [ ] **Session 9 scoring**: Can response structure hold three score fields?
- [ ] **Extensibility**: Easy to add new fields without breaking changes?

### Testing Integration
- [ ] **Test database**: Tests use separate DB or same DB as dev?
- [ ] **Fixtures**: Are there shared fixtures for test data?
- [ ] **Test isolation**: Tests can run in parallel or must be serial?

---

## Test Coverage Review

### Endpoint Tests
- [ ] **Happy path**: All three endpoints tested successfully?
- [ ] **Pagination**: Tests verify limit/offset work correctly?
- [ ] **Sorting**: Test verifies stories are correctly sorted?
- [ ] **Boundary**: Test limit=0, limit=1000, offset=-1, offset=999999?

### Error Cases
- [ ] **404 tests**: Story ID that doesn't exist returns 404?
- [ ] **Invalid params**: Non-integer ID returns 422?
- [ ] **Database error**: Simulated DB failure returns 500 with proper error?

### Data Integrity
- [ ] **Comment ordering**: Comments returned in logical order (chronological? threaded)?
- [ ] **Completeness**: All fields from schema are returned?
- [ ] **NULL handling**: Null fields handled (e.g., story without URL)?

**Request Example Tests**:
```python
def test_stories_sorted_correctly():
    response = client.get("/stories?limit=10")
    stories = response.json()
    # Check score descending, then time descending
    for i in range(len(stories) - 1):
        assert (stories[i]["score"], stories[i]["time"]) >= \
               (stories[i+1]["score"], stories[i+1]["time"])

def test_story_not_found():
    response = client.get("/stories/999999999")
    assert response.status_code == 404
    assert "not found" in response.json()["detail"].lower()

def test_comments_form_valid_tree():
    response = client.get("/stories/123/comments")
    comments = response.json()
    # Every parent_id must reference existing comment
    comment_ids = {c["id"] for c in comments}
    for comment in comments:
        if comment["parent_id"]:
            assert comment["parent_id"] in comment_ids
`

records.title: Support Multi-Root and Intersecting Graph Configurations
records.body:
# Description:
The current graph configuration format in the project assumes a tree structure with a single root and no overlapping branches. This limits the expressiveness and applicability of the engine for complex workflows that require:
- Multiple entry points (multi-root graphs)
- Shared subgraphs (intersecting branches)
- Arbitrary DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) structures

To support broader use cases, a new configuration format should be introduced that allows for general DAG definitions, while ensuring safety through automatic cycle detection.

## Proposal:
- Design and implement a new version of the graph configuration format that supports:
- Multiple root nodes
- Node reuse across different branches
- Non-tree DAGs with converging paths
- Add a cycle detection mechanism to prevent invalid (cyclic) graphs
- Update the parser, validators, and runtime execution logic accordingly
- Ensure backward compatibility with the existing configuration format, or provide a migration path

## Benefits:
- Enables more flexible and realistic workflow modeling
- Supports advanced scenarios such as conditional branching, shared enrichment steps, and post-processing joins
- Improves reusability and reduces configuration duplication

## Next Steps:
1. Define the specification for the new configuration format (YAML/JSON schema or DSL syntax)
2. Implement graph validator with cycle detection (e.g., using DFS or topological sort)
3. Refactor graph builder and runtime to support generalized DAGs
